title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature
authors: Xuanlyu Zhu, Feng Tian, Yang Zhong, Pengqi Zheng, Xiwen Bi, Ling Luo
abstract: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.

infographic.key_insight: The best system scored 0.7389 on patient-specific phenotype recognition from full-text biomedical literature, exceeding the baseline by 8.37 percentage points.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Linking phenotype concepts to the correct patients could support rare disease research and genotype–phenotype analysis, but clinical utility was not evaluated.
method: Recognize phenotype concepts across full-text biomedical articles.
Associate extracted phenotype concepts with specific patients.
Top teams explored biomedical language models, LLMs, and ensemble strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark used 200 annotated PatientPheX articles containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient–phenotype associations.
infographic.watch_item: Patient attribution and phenotype normalization remain challenging, especially in articles describing multiple patients.
infographic.paper_title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature

title: Visualizing and Interpreting Temporal Care Team Dynamics for Cancer Survival Risk Analysis
authors: Yuhua Huang, Hsiao-Ying Lu, Kwan-Liu Ma
abstract: Cancer care is a longitudinal, time-sensitive process requiring coordination among diverse healthcare professionals (HCPs), whose collaboration evolves throughout treatment. Prior studies link care team structure to patient outcomes, but the temporal dynamics of collaboration and their relationship to evolving patient risk remain poorly understood. We introduce a visual analytics framework for modeling and interpreting time-varying care team interactions in oncology. We construct dynamic collaboration networks from electronic health record (EHR)-mediated communication data and use a temporal graph neural network (TGNN) to estimate patient outcome risk over time. We then investigate how changes in care team composition and specialist participation relate to shifts in estimated risk across treatment stages. Our multi-view interactive system combines TGNN-based risk modeling with coordinated visualizations of care team networks, feature-level explanations from a surrogate logistic regression model, and exploratory what-if analysis. Without making causal claims, the system helps analysts examine how risk estimates co-evolve with collaboration patterns and identify care team characteristics associated with these changes. We demonstrate its utility through expert-guided analysis scenarios involving 505 patients with breast, colorectal, and lung cancers, evaluating its ability to reveal clinically meaningful collaboration patterns. This work improves the interpretability of temporal graph-based models in longitudinal, team-based healthcare, with potential applicability to other evolving collaborative settings.

infographic.key_insight: A visual analytics framework links evolving cancer care team collaboration patterns with model-estimated patient outcome risk, without implying causation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system may help analysts explore how care team composition and specialist participation relate to estimated risk across treatment stages.
method: Build dynamic care team networks from EHR-mediated communications.
Estimate risk over time using a temporal graph neural network.
Combine interactive network views, surrogate logistic regression explanations, and exploratory what-if analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Expert-guided analysis scenarios covered 505 patients with breast, colorectal, and lung cancers; the abstract reports no quantitative predictive performance.
infographic.watch_item: Observed associations and exploratory what-if results do not establish that changing care team structure would improve patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Visualizing and Interpreting Temporal Care Team Dynamics for Cancer Survival Risk Analysis

title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Ronald Fecso, José Morano, Botond Fazekas, Paul Widmann-Sedlnitzky, Dorota Himel, Laetita Hinterhuber
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Retinal OCT finding recognition outpaced visual localization: the best general-purpose model achieved 23.7% grounding macro F1, rising to 33.9% with OCT-specific RetGrounder.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Localizing reported retinal abnormalities is important for assessing whether AI image interpretations are grounded in visible findings.
method: Created RetinaGroundBench with ophthalmologist-annotated bounding boxes for retinal OCT biomarkers.
Introduced AggIoU to assess coverage when models split a lesion across multiple predicted boxes.
Evaluated 27 open-source MLLMs and fine-tuned the 8B RetGrounder using grounding and textual information.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark includes 815 B-scans, 4,537 bounding boxes, 13 biomarkers and 8 diseases; RetGrounder improved grounding F1 by 43% relative to the best general-purpose model.
infographic.watch_item: Grounding performance remains limited, and the abstract does not establish clinical deployment readiness or generalization beyond this benchmark.
infographic.paper_title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models

title: The Value of System 1 Models in Medicine
authors: Xiufeng Yang, Konstantinos Vrettos, Zeineb Ben Chaaben, Fabian Drexel, Jannik Lübberstedt, Johannes Moll
abstract: Many clinical decisions are a choice among a few fixed options, taken quickly and in large numbers. Such decisions also need an uncertainty estimate to know when to defer to a clinician. Generative language models answer slowly in free text and state their confidence poorly. In contrast, System 1 models answer zero-shot with a probability for each answer. However, their performance across clinical tasks is unknown. Four System 1 models, two proprietary and two with open weights, were evaluated zero-shot on 86 public tasks from 14 clinical domains in 20 languages, spanning examination questions and medical imaging. Tasks were assigned to six capability tiers before analysis. The primary outcome was the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary outcomes included calibration, language effects and comparisons with published results and generative models. Across 179,111 cases, the mean AUROC of the best model per task was 0.94 for medical knowledge, 0.93 for text understanding, 0.83 for clinical judgement from text, 0.89 for image perception, 0.84 for 2D image findings and 0.69 for volumetric findings. Imaging tasks scored 0.09 (95% CI, 0.06 to 0.11) lower than text tasks (P < 0.001). The best model matched or exceeded the best published result on 13 of 26 text tasks and on 8 of 35 imaging tasks. Triage nurses outperformed the best model (accuracy, 0.85 vs. 0.56). One decision took 0.34 to 0.44 seconds and 24 to 81 joules on open-weight models run locally. Accuracy on identical questions fell by up to 39 percentage points from English to Yoruba. Generative models of the same family were 11 to 76 times slower, with 3 to 5 percentage points higher balanced accuracy. System 1 models decide quickly, cheaply and with usable confidence when the answer is stated in a text or recalled from medical knowledge, but not when it must be judged or read from an image.

infographic.key_insight: System 1 models made fast, probability-based decisions but performed better on medical knowledge and text understanding than on clinical judgement or imaging.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These models may support narrowly defined fixed-choice tasks, but the results do not establish readiness for autonomous clinical use.
method: Evaluated four models zero-shot on 86 public tasks across 14 clinical domains and 20 languages.
Grouped tasks into six capability tiers, with AUROC as the primary outcome.
Assessed calibration, language effects, speed and comparisons with published results and generative models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 179,111 cases, mean AUROC for the best model per task ranged from 0.94 for medical knowledge to 0.69 for volumetric findings; imaging scored 0.09 below text.
infographic.watch_item: Performance varied substantially by task and language: triage nurses outperformed the best model, and accuracy fell by up to 39 percentage points from English to Yoruba.
infographic.paper_title: The Value of System 1 Models in Medicine

title: From Structured Records to Patient Narratives: Preserving Clinical Alignment in LLM-Generated Health Summaries
authors: Bayram Ayadi, Florian Geissler, Johanna Schmidhuber
abstract: As wearable and digital health systems increasingly generate longitudinal physiological records, communicating these observations in patient-accessible language remains a significant challenge. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising mechanism for translating structured clinical information into readable narratives, but this process may introduce semantic drift, where clinically precise meaning is distorted during simplification. We investigate evidence-grounded health summarization for menstrual health monitoring using a constrained generation framework that combines structured evidence conditioning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using a prompt-based constrained generation framework. We evaluate semantic alignment using Natural Language Inference (NLI), atomic factuality metrics, and readability measures. Across three LLMs and 4,500 generated summaries, explicit grounding constraints consistently improve clinical alignment, particularly by improving uncertainty preservation and, once faithfulness is evaluated against retrieved evidence, generally preserving or improving faithfulness, while effects on omission remain model-dependent. We also find that improved clinical alignment comes at the cost of increased reading difficulty and medical terminology. These findings highlight the need to jointly evaluate faithfulness, uncertainty preservation, and readability when developing patient-facing medical LLM systems.

infographic.key_insight: Explicit evidence-grounding constraints improved clinical alignment in LLM-generated menstrual health summaries, but made them harder to read.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Patient-facing health summaries need to preserve clinical meaning and uncertainty while remaining understandable.
method: Generated menstrual health narratives from structured records using a prompt-based constrained framework.
Combined structured evidence conditioning with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
Evaluated alignment with natural language inference, atomic factuality metrics, and readability measures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three LLMs and 4,500 summaries, grounding improved uncertainty preservation and generally maintained or improved faithfulness when evaluated against retrieved evidence; omission effects varied by model.
infographic.watch_item: Greater alignment came with harder reading and more medical terminology; the abstract does not establish patient comprehension or clinical benefit.
infographic.paper_title: From Structured Records to Patient Narratives: Preserving Clinical Alignment in LLM-Generated Health Summaries

title: IndoNutriQA: An Indonesian Clinical Nutrition Question Answering Benchmark
authors: Tirana Noor Fatyanosa, Ummu Ditya Erliana, Mahendra Data, Muhammad Nurwegiono, Eleazar Tadeo Eman, Alham Fikri Aji
abstract: Clinical Question Answering (QA) underpins Clinical Intelligent Decision Support Systems, but progress is severely limited for low-resource languages such as Indonesian by the absence of public domain-specific data. We introduce IndoNutriQA, an expert-curated Indonesian clinical QA benchmark of 911 question-answer pairs built from real clinical-nutrition reports. Rather than a large-scale training corpus, it is positioned as a high-quality evaluation resource: every pair is grounded in a clinically relevant context, enriched with structured metadata (anthropometric assessment, medical diagnosis, document provenance, chunk segmentation). Eight standardised question types following the Nutrition Care Process (NCP), including the Problem, Etiology, Sign and Symptom (PES) diagnosis statement, are answered for every report, which was written by a graduate-level dietetic intern, by one of three nutritionists. Answers are free-form clinical prose rather than extractive spans, and an expert validation study finds 6-10% of reference answers contestable. The dataset supports generative, extractive and retrieval-augmented QA as well as zero- and few-shot LLM evaluation. We report fine-tuned baselines (IndoBERT variants, mT5, RAG) with 5-fold cross-validation, learning curves and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and benchmark eight contemporary LLMs zero- and five-shot. We further calibrate our LLM-as-judge rubric against three expert raters (one RD, two nutritionists), finding it human-comparable on factuality and completeness but unreliable on clinical safety, and a human error analysis shows it misses unsupported content that the raters identify. IndoNutriQA is released to foster research in Indonesian clinical NLP and nutritional decision support.

infographic.key_insight: IndoNutriQA introduces an expert-curated benchmark for evaluating Indonesian clinical nutrition question answering in a low-resource language.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark supports research toward Indonesian nutritional decision support, but does not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Curated 911 question–answer pairs from real clinical nutrition reports, with structured metadata.
Used eight standardized Nutrition Care Process question types and free-form answers from nutritionists.
Evaluated fine-tuned baselines with 5-fold cross-validation and eight LLMs in zero- and five-shot settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Expert validation found 6–10% of reference answers contestable; an LLM judge was human-comparable on factuality and completeness but unreliable on clinical safety.
infographic.watch_item: Automated scoring missed unsupported content identified by human raters, underscoring the need for expert safety review.
infographic.paper_title: IndoNutriQA: An Indonesian Clinical Nutrition Question Answering Benchmark

title: GWDM: A Guided Wavelet Diffusion Model for Realistic Histopathology Image Generation
authors: Abdullah, Tao Huang, Ickjai Lee, Lei Bi, Euijoon Ahn
abstract: Histopathology images are recognized as a reliable and comprehensive modality for Deep Learning (DL) based diagnosis. However, effectiveness is constrained by limited large-scale annotated datasets, as collecting expert-labeled medical data is costly and time-intensive. Recent advances in generative models, particularly diffusion models, demonstrate strong capabilities in synthesizing medically relevant content for dataset augmentation. Existing generative frameworks treat histopathology patches as generic natural images, failing to enforce biological constraints such as histomorphological structures and heterogeneous staining patterns essential for valid synthesis. We propose a guided wavelet diffusion model (GWDM) framework that captures image details at multiple scales using wavelets and leverages controllable conditioning based on domain-specific histopathological features (e.g., tissue patterns and color variations). We further formulate a histomorphological guidance loss applied to real and generated patches. A loss ramping strategy gradually introduces these constraints during training, ensuring stable optimization and robust modeling of tissue architecture. GWDM was evaluated on three benchmark datasets (BCSS, MoNuSeg, and PAIP2019), consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative methods. Ablation studies confirmed that domain-guided conditioning, perceptual loss, and structural similarity loss each contribute meaningfully to synthesis quality. Downstream nuclei and tissue segmentation experiments further validated the clinical utility of GWDM-generated images, demonstrating consistent performance improvements when synthetic data augments real training sets. This work shows that domain-specific conditioning and dual-loss optimization generate realistic histopathology patches, reducing data scarcity and improving clinical downstream segmentation performance.

infographic.key_insight: GWDM combines wavelet-based diffusion with histopathology-specific guidance to generate realistic tissue image patches for training-data augmentation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Synthetic patches improved downstream nuclei and tissue segmentation in benchmark experiments, suggesting potential value for research on data-limited pathology AI.
method: Use wavelets to capture image details at multiple scales.
Condition generation on tissue patterns and staining variations.
Gradually introduce histomorphological guidance using perceptual and structural similarity losses.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across BCSS, MoNuSeg, and PAIP2019, the abstract reports better synthesis than state-of-the-art methods and segmentation gains when synthetic images augmented real training data.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark improvements do not establish clinical readiness; synthetic-image fidelity and generalization across laboratories require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: GWDM: A Guided Wavelet Diffusion Model for Realistic Histopathology Image Generation

title: Automated screening of privacy risks in medical AI
authors: Konstantinos Vrettos, Eleftherios Tzanis, Haridimos Kondylakis, Evangelia E. Vassalou, Florence X. Doo, Michail E. Klontzas
abstract: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) models are often shared without their training data, assuming this protects the patients who contributed them. However, a model can reveal whether a patient's records were used in training, a privacy breach known as a membership inference attack. This risk is usually reported as a cohort average, which can appear negligible while individual patients are almost certainly exposed. Identifying potentially vulnerable records before developing a production model could make privacy assessment more practical. We measured each patient's vulnerability to membership inference attack, across 7,789 models trained on six clinical datasets in four modalities, including two adapted pretrained medical models. Training choices changed how many patients had high attack scores, but the patients who ranked highest by risk largely stayed the same across the configurations we tested. Stronger weight decay reduced the exposed cohort up to threefold, yet largely the same patients remained most at risk across training recipes, architectures and initializations, including foundation models. Therefore, we developed a lightweight screening tool that uses four small models to identify patients with high risk of exposure before production-model training. We also assessed if flagged patients could be protected without removing their data. Privacy screening should become incorporated into data preparation for clinical AI.

infographic.key_insight: Patients at highest risk of having their training-set membership exposed remained largely consistent across tested medical AI configurations, enabling lightweight early screening.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Screening during data preparation could flag patient records at elevated privacy risk that cohort-average assessments may obscure.
method: Measured patient-level vulnerability to membership inference attacks across training configurations.
Tested how weight decay, architectures and initializations affected exposure risk.
Developed a screening tool using four small models before production-model training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered 7,789 models across six clinical datasets and four modalities, including two adapted pretrained medical models; stronger weight decay reduced the exposed cohort up to threefold.
infographic.watch_item: Screening flags potential vulnerability rather than guaranteeing privacy protection; performance beyond the tested datasets and configurations remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Automated screening of privacy risks in medical AI

title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge
authors: Min Zeng, Zaifu Zhan, Kai Yu, Rui Zhang
abstract: Medical knowledge evolves as clinical guidelines revise recommendations, yet whether large language models (LLMs) faithfully incorporate such changes remains unclear. We introduce ChronoEvo, comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from incorporation into clinical recommendations. In the primary model, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions and 80.2% were clinically correct, but only 58.5% fully incorporated guidance, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point recognition-incorporation gap. This dissociation persisted across 14 models and was corroborated by two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses, yielding a 40.3-percentage-point gap in the validation sample. Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were associated with retention of outdated guidance. A revision-salience intervention reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness but did not significantly improve full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of evolving medical knowledge as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability, even when updated guideline evidence is available.

infographic.key_insight: Recognizing updated medical guidance did not ensure faithful incorporation: the primary model recognized 90.8% of revisions but fully incorporated only 58.5%.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Clinical LLM outputs may retain outdated recommendations even when updated guideline evidence is available.
method: Introduced ChronoEvo with 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 types of medical knowledge change.
Evaluated recognition and incorporation across 14 models, with two-clinician adjudication of 300 responses.
Tested a revision-salience intervention to emphasize updated guidance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The primary model showed a 32.3-percentage-point recognition–incorporation gap; clinician-adjudicated validation found a 40.3-point gap.
infographic.watch_item: Emphasizing revisions reduced outdated content and improved clinical correctness, but did not significantly improve full incorporation.
infographic.paper_title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge

title: Privacy-Preserving Large Language Model Deployment for Oncology Registry Abstraction: Structure-Aware Evaluation in a Real-World Clinical Setting
authors: Moldovan, M.; Enikeev, R.; Chu, M.; Amalraj, A.; Koli, P. P.; Abdul, S. S.; Sivaraj, H.; Iqbal, U.; Toh, C. K.
abstract:
Objectives Structuring oncology clinical notes into registry-grade variables is essential for research and care but remains labour-intensive and error-prone. This study developed and evaluated a privacy-preserving large language model pipeline for oncology registry abstraction in a real-world clinical setting.
Methods An open-source Meta Llama 3.3 70B-based pipeline, prompted without task-specific fine-tuning, was deployed to extract over 50 variables from 6,700 oncology notes at a cancer centre in Singapore. Data were de-identified locally using a Hide-In-Plain-Sight approach, ensuring no identifiable data left hospital infrastructure. Performance was assessed on 200 randomly sampled notes with adjudicated ground truth, using a structure-aware framework that classified outputs as correct, missing, spurious, or incorrect.
Results F1 scores were high across variables, including diagnosis (97.2%), histology (95.8%), stage (92.6%), biomarkers (91.4%), and treatments (88.1%). Preliminary transferability testing on 50 external notes showed strong performance for core diagnostic variables, with reduced performance for list-valued variables.
Discussion The structure-aware evaluation approach separated omissions from fabrications, providing more clinically actionable insight than aggregate metrics alone.
Conclusion Privacy-preserving large language models achieved high extraction accuracy under a clinician-verified reference standard, supporting their feasibility for oncology registry abstraction in real-world clinical settings. Keywords: Large language models; Oncology registry abstraction; Natural language processing; Privacy-preserving AI; Clinical data extraction
What is already known on this topic Structuring oncology clinical notes into registry-grade variables is essential for cancer research and care but remains labour-intensive, costly, and inconsistent from one reviewer to the next when performed manually. Large language models offer potential to automate this task, but their use in real-world registries has been limited by concerns over patient data privacy, reliance on task-specific fine-tuning, and evaluation methods that obscure the difference between missing and fabricated information.
What this study adds This study shows that an open-source, privacy-preserving large language model pipeline, deployed entirely within hospital infrastructure without task-specific fine-tuning, can extract over 50 registry variables from oncology notes with high accuracy (F1 scores 88-97% across key variables), validated against ground truth checked by two clinicians. Using a structure-aware evaluation framework, we demonstrate that errors can be meaningfully separated into missing, spurious, and incorrect categories, offering clearer insight into model behaviour than aggregate accuracy metrics alone, and show preliminary evidence of transferability to notes from an external setting.
How this study might affect research, practice or policy These findings support the feasibility of deploying privacy-preserving, locally hosted large language models for oncology registry abstraction without requiring identifiable data to leave hospital systems or extensive model customisation. The structure-aware evaluation framework is also shared as a reusable template, enabling other institutions to validate similar AI extraction tools in a consistent, clinically meaningful way before wider implementation.

infographic.key_insight: A privacy-preserving Llama 3.3 70B pipeline extracted oncology registry variables with high F1 scores without task-specific fine-tuning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could reduce manual registry abstraction workload while keeping identifiable patient data within hospital infrastructure.
method: Processed 6,700 oncology notes at a Singapore cancer centre to extract over 50 variables.
Used local Hide-In-Plain-Sight de-identification before LLM extraction.
Evaluated outputs as correct, missing, spurious, or incorrect against adjudicated reference data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on 200 randomly sampled notes yielded F1 scores of 97.2% for diagnosis, 95.8% for histology, 92.6% for stage, 91.4% for biomarkers, and 88.1% for treatments.
infographic.watch_item: External testing was preliminary, involving only 50 notes, and showed reduced performance for list-valued variables.
infographic.paper_title: Privacy-Preserving Large Language Model Deployment for Oncology Registry Abstraction: Structure-Aware Evaluation in a Real-World Clinical Setting

title: RetiJev: Fast and Source-Grounded Ophthalmic Decision Models
authors: Bo Liu, Lianyu Wang, Meng Wang, Ching-Yu Cheng, Huazhu Fu
abstract: Ophthalmic clinical decision support requires fast, accurate, and privacy-preserving inference, yet autoregressive large language models (LLMs) incur substantial latency and computational overhead for decisions among predefined actions. We therefore investigate a decision-oriented alternative to generative reasoning. Specifically, we first introduce RetiJev-Data, a source-grounded ophthalmology corpus comprising 78,158 clinical-decision and diagnosis questions derived from articles in PubMed Central and a MeSH vocabulary covering 531 eye diseases, and 50,074 guideline-grading questions spanning 11 grading systems, along with a 24,662-question evaluation benchmark. Based on this, we develop RetiJev, a family of 0.8B-9B decision models that directly score candidate answers without autoregressive decoding. Across all model sizes, RetiJev outperforms both a 27B LLM and the commercial Jev 1.13 decision model on guideline grading by 10.4-23.0 points. RetiJev-9B further achieves the highest accuracy on clinical decisions, improving over both baselines by 5.4-6.5 points while matching them on diagnosis. It answers a case in 158 ms on one GPU, 3.5x faster than LLM generation and 470x faster than reasoning. Models are released at https://github.com/Awenbocc/RetiJev.

infographic.key_insight: RetiJev directly scores predefined answers, outperforming larger baselines on ophthalmic guideline grading while avoiding autoregressive generation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Fast, locally deployable decision models could support ophthalmic workflows, but clinical benefit and deployment safety remain unestablished.
method: Built source-grounded questions from PubMed Central articles, a 531-eye-disease MeSH vocabulary, and 11 grading systems.
Developed 0.8B–9B models that score candidate answers without generating reasoning text.
Compared accuracy and inference speed with a 27B LLM and Jev 1.13.
infographic.evidence_signal: The corpus contains 128,232 questions plus a 24,662-question evaluation benchmark; reported guideline-grading gains were 10.4–23.0 points, and RetiJev-9B answered a case in 158 ms on one GPU.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish real-world clinical safety; predefined answer choices and deployment-specific privacy safeguards require validation.
infographic.paper_title: RetiJev: Fast and Source-Grounded Ophthalmic Decision Models

title: ViBMR: A Large-Scale Multi-Sequence Brain MRI Dataset and Comprehensive Evaluation for Vietnamese Radiology Report Generation
authors: Dai Lam Le, Minh Khoi Nguyen, Son Dinh Nguyen, Amir Reza Jafari, Viet Ha, Nguyen Son
abstract: Automated radiology report generation for multi-sequence brain MRI holds strong promise for alleviating radiologists' workload, yet it remains a demanding problem: brain MRI studies are inherently volumetric, each pulse sequence carries complementary diagnostic information, and annotated data are critically scarce for low-resource clinical languages. Existing brain MRI-report resources are still dominated by English reports, translated clinical text, or datasets adapted from task-specific imaging benchmarks, leaving routine low-resource clinical reporting and heterogeneous multi-sequence MRI protocols insufficiently represented. To bridge this gap, we introduce ViBMR, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale multi-sequence brain MRI dataset paired with routine Vietnamese clinical reports, comprising 3,649 patients and 11,875 MRI series across T1, T2, FLAIR, and contrast-enhanced T1 sequences. Building on ViBMR, we establish a comprehensive evaluation setup for brain MRI report generation, covering representative medical vision-language models, multi-sequence inputs, and feature aggregation strategies. The results provide key insights into dataset characteristics and model behavior, while demonstrating the necessity of native low-resource clinical datasets for reliable Vietnamese-origin brain MRI report generation. Our dataset and baseline models will be released for non-commercial research.

infographic.key_insight: ViBMR introduces a large-scale dataset pairing multi-sequence brain MRI with routine Vietnamese reports to support report-generation research in a low-resource clinical language.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The resource could support research toward reducing radiologists’ reporting workload, but clinical reliability is not established by the abstract.
method: Pair brain MRI studies with routine Vietnamese clinical reports.
Include T1, T2, FLAIR, and contrast-enhanced T1 sequences.
Evaluate representative medical vision-language models, multi-sequence inputs, and feature aggregation strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The dataset contains 3,649 patients and 11,875 MRI series; the abstract describes comprehensive benchmarking but reports no numerical performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Generalizability and clinical safety require further validation before use in patient care.
infographic.paper_title: ViBMR: A Large-Scale Multi-Sequence Brain MRI Dataset and Comprehensive Evaluation for Vietnamese Radiology Report Generation

title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection
authors: Ghulam Mudassir, Hameed Ullah Khan, Ahmad Sami Al-Shamayleh, Muhammad Faizan Khan, Muhammad Muqtasid, Moamin Abughazala
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has several transformative effects on healthcare, like to facilitate clinicians in disease detection and to manage patient care with enhanced precision. Due to the increasing complexity of medical data and the growing volume of diagnostic images, the substantial computational power needed to process such information creates both opportunities and challenges. To accomplish this objective, numerous methodologies have been proposed to integrate AI into disease detection systems. All these methodologies consider different aspects of clinical diagnosis, considering key parameters such as the type of AI model employed, the nature of input data, and the population demographics being analysed. In this paper, we review different state-of-the-art techniques which have been proposed for various areas of disease detection, specifically focusing on bias identification and mitigation. The proposed solutions are distinguished based on the type of input data they utilize, the architecture of model, and type of bias (algorithmic bias, demographic bias, model bias, and deployment bias). The time frame chosen to filter out relevant studies is between 2015 and 2026. Eventually, we review 23 related articles out of 64,389 analyzed from seven different digital libraries. The obtained results guide us to reach a conclusion with respect to state-of-the-art selected studies. Furthermore, these results reveal significant research gaps that can assist researchers in addressing AI-related bias in medical diagnosis. By prioritizing explainability, data diversity, and fairness in algorithmic design, as well as equitable access for affected patient populations, they can utilize available healthcare resources more effectively.

infographic.key_insight: This review maps bias in AI disease detection and highlights explainability, data diversity, and fairness-aware design as priorities for more equitable systems.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Bias in diagnostic AI may produce uneven performance across patient populations, making fairness assessment important before clinical deployment.
method: Reviewed disease-detection AI literature within a stated 2015–2026 search window.
Selected 23 articles from 64,389 records analyzed across seven digital libraries.
Categorized approaches by input data, model architecture, and algorithmic, demographic, model, or deployment bias.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a literature review of 23 selected articles but provides no quantitative estimates of diagnostic performance or bias reduction.
infographic.watch_item: The review identifies priorities rather than demonstrating that any specific mitigation strategy reliably improves fairness in clinical practice.
infographic.paper_title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection

title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
authors: Jiayan Yang, Ad Feelders, Arno Siebes
abstract: Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays. This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. Instead of relying on naive deterministic aggregation or fixed safety buffers, the framework explicitly models dynamic predictive uncertainty and evaluates extreme shortage exposure using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). These aggregated, risk-calibrated demand signals are then embedded into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy to generate delay-constrained staffing decisions. Evaluated on realistic trajectories from the MIMIC-IV database, the proposed framework demonstrates a favorable cost-shortage trade-off compared to deterministic and purely reactive baselines. Pareto frontier analysis illustrates how uncertainty-aware demand construction changes resource allocation under varying safety preferences, while stress testing confirms the framework's operational robustness even when subjected to systematic predictive bias in the form of calibration drift. By formalizing this translation layer, this work provides a principled, transparent pathway for safely integrating probabilistic AI outputs into high-stakes healthcare operational systems.

infographic.key_insight: An uncertainty-aware framework translates predicted patient risks into ICU staffing plans, reporting a favorable balance between staffing costs and shortages.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support ICU staffing decisions under shift rigidity and hiring delays, but patient-outcome benefits remain unproven.
method: Model dynamic predictive uncertainty without changing the upstream risk model.
Use Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) to assess extreme staffing-shortage exposure.
Feed risk-calibrated demand into hourly rolling-horizon scheduling with staffing delays.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on realistic MIMIC-IV trajectories compared cost–shortage trade-offs against deterministic and reactive baselines, with Pareto analysis and calibration-drift stress tests.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports retrospective trajectory-based evaluation, not prospective evidence of staffing feasibility or patient safety benefits.
infographic.paper_title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing

title: Expandable Modality Experts for Medical Vision-Language Learning
authors: DM BAPPY, Eunsu Kim, Hanjoo Lee, Sung Hak Lee, Sangjeong Ahn
abstract: Learning across medical imaging modalities requires making use of images without paired text and accommodating new domains while retaining existing representations. We propose a medical vision-language technique built around an expandable bank of modality experts. Its Multiway Transformer combines shared visual computation with deterministically routed feed-forward experts and a separate text pathway. A modality-aware visual tokenizer supplies targets for masked pretraining on 19.4 million unpaired image rows across seven modalities; contrastive alignment then uses 3.23 million image-text pairs. Additional fundus and optical coherence tomography experts learn from paired data while the original image and text embedding paths remain frozen. With a ViT-Large backbone, the proposed technique achieves the best or tied-best result in 24 of 25 benchmark settings across nine modalities: 10 of 11 zero-shot classification benchmarks, all 10 linear probes, and all four retrieval benchmarks. Mean balanced accuracy is 0.674 for zero-shot classification and 0.856 for linear probing, and mean bidirectional retrieval recall is 20.70%. A separate three-seed sequential experiment with matched adaptation data yields fundus and OCT retrieval gains of 14.95 and 9.31 percentage points, with no measured loss on preceding fundus or pathology tasks. The preservation argument requires unchanged existing computation paths and inference conditions, and feature-identity checks verify retention on evaluated inputs. The proposed technique provides a modular approach to learning and expanding medical vision-language representations.

infographic.key_insight: An expandable bank of modality-specific experts enables medical vision-language learning across imaging types while preserving existing representations under unchanged computation paths and inference conditions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support reusable image classification and retrieval tools across medical imaging modalities, but clinical utility has not been established.
method: Combine shared visual computation with modality-routed experts and a separate text pathway.
Pretrain on unpaired images with modality-aware masked targets, then align image-text pairs.
Add fundus and OCT experts while freezing existing image and text embedding paths.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 19.4 million unpaired image rows and 3.23 million image-text pairs, the model achieved best or tied-best results in 24 of 25 benchmark settings across nine modalities.
infographic.watch_item: Retention depends on unchanged existing computation paths and inference conditions; feature-identity checks verify it only on evaluated inputs.
infographic.paper_title: Expandable Modality Experts for Medical Vision-Language Learning

title: Are Joint-Embedding Predictive Objectives Effective for Longitudinal EHRs?
authors: Ashvin Gupta, Brendan Delaney, Alessandra Russo
abstract: Masked language modelling (MLM) is the dominant pretraining objective for transformer encoders applied to longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). However, reconstructing individual events may overemphasise noisy or weakly informative observations and does not explicitly encourage learning higher-level patient states. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) instead learn by predicting representations in latent space and have shown strong performance in a variety of domains. In this paper, we investigate to what extent JEPA can be adapted to EHR sequence representation. Our empirical investigation using MIMIC-IV shows that although all three of our JEPA formulations train stably without representational collapse, they consistently underperform standard MLM. We find that target size, not target heterogeneity, increases prediction error, yet reducing the target size does not recover downstream performance. This suggests that stable latent prediction alone is insufficient for competitive EHR representation learning and highlights the challenge of defining clinically meaningful latent targets for EHR.

infographic.key_insight: Three joint-embedding predictive formulations trained stably on longitudinal EHRs but consistently underperformed standard masked language modelling.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Stable latent-space learning alone did not yield competitive patient representations in this study, limiting its promise for downstream clinical AI tasks.
method: Adapted three Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) formulations to longitudinal EHR sequences.
Compared latent-representation prediction with masked language modelling.
Examined how target size and heterogeneity affected prediction error.
infographic.evidence_signal: In MIMIC-IV experiments, all three JEPA formulations avoided representational collapse, but reducing target size did not recover downstream performance.
infographic.watch_item: Results from MIMIC-IV may not generalize to other EHR settings; defining clinically meaningful latent targets remains a challenge.
infographic.paper_title: Are Joint-Embedding Predictive Objectives Effective for Longitudinal EHRs?

title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report
authors: Soumya Ranjan Sahoo, Divya Bharti, Sanand Sasidharan
abstract: Electronic health records are written to support care, not retrieval. Across years of oncology notes, the primary diagnosis is restated in report after report, while the events that shape a patient's course, such as a recurrence or a change in therapy, may be recorded only once. A retriever that ranks passages by similarity to the query keeps returning the repeated material and can miss these transitions, that is, it exhibits temporal redundancy across historical narratives. We argue that longitudinal clinical retrieval should be treated as allocating a limited evidence budget across time, not just ranking by relevance. We separate the task into three objectives: temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation. In Study A (13 clinical queries over 20 patient records, with two-stage reconstruction), the Temporal-15 configuration reaches a milestone slot recall of 0.538, compared with 0.388 for the Global-50 baseline. However, it also retrieves far more evidence (496 versus 50 indexed units per query), so the gain cannot be credited to allocation alone. When evidence is held fixed, removing prompted precedence rules raises schema-order reversals from 0.010 to 0.080. A five-patient, single-query pilot with fixed budgets finds that wider temporal coverage does not reliably yield more dated milestones. Together, these results suggest that how much a record says about a period is a poor guide to how useful that period is as evidence. Because no expert reference timelines are available, our measurements describe retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy. This position and technical report presents the retrieval analysis behind the Onco-CONSTRUE framework and sets out a research agenda for budget-constrained longitudinal clinical retrieval.

infographic.key_insight: Longitudinal clinical retrieval should allocate limited evidence across time rather than repeatedly retrieve similar passages that may obscure key transitions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Retrieving less-repeated events, such as recurrence or therapy changes, could support more informative oncology timelines, but clinical accuracy remains unvalidated.
method: Separate temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation.
Compare Temporal-15 with Global-50 retrieval using two-stage timeline reconstruction.
Test prompted precedence rules and fixed-budget temporal coverage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 13 queries over 20 patient records, Temporal-15 achieved milestone slot recall of 0.538 versus 0.388 for Global-50, while retrieving 496 versus 50 indexed units per query.
infographic.watch_item: Unequal retrieval budgets confound the recall gain, and absent expert reference timelines, results measure retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report

title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions
authors: Marcos Matabuena, Xiaokai Luo, Oscar Hernan Madrid Padilla
abstract: Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.

infographic.key_insight: A deep learning framework predicts complex outcomes directly in metric spaces without requiring manifold assumptions or Euclidean embeddings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support digital biomarker research by predicting distribution-valued outcomes from accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data.
method: Uses the response space’s metric structure for regression with random objects.
Establishes statistical consistency and convergence rates under stated assumptions.
Identifies conditions for mitigating dimensionality challenges in hierarchically compositional regression.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations showed competitive performance and gains over several comparators in multiple settings, alongside two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish clinical utility; theoretical guarantees depend on stated assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions

title: An interpretable deep learning method for early hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis on multiphase CT
authors: Emma Sarfati, Alexandre Bône, Pietro Gori, Sisi Yang, Marc-Michel Rohé, François Nicolas
abstract: Early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma is critical to preserve access to curative treatment options. The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) provides a standardized framework for non-invasive diagnosis on multiphase computed tomography, based on major visual imaging features. However, these features may be difficult to assess consistently, particularly in small liver lesions. We developed dLI-RADS, an interpretable artificial intelligence method designed to estimate the probability of hepatocellular carcinoma from multiphase computed tomography images of manually segmented liver lesions, while remaining aligned with LI-RADS-related imaging concepts. dLI-RADS combines neural network-derived predictions with handcrafted quantitative imaging measurements reflecting LI-RADS major features and integrates these inputs using logistic regression. In this multicenter retrospective study, patients with multiphase computed tomography and at least one liver lesion were included, while lesions larger than 40 mm were excluded. Histology served as the reference standard for hepatocellular carcinoma, and a composite reference standard was used for non-hepatocellular carcinoma lesions. The lesion-level accuracy of dLI-RADS and LI-RADS were compared on the internal evaluation set using 10,000-repetition bootstrap non-inferiority tests, with 5% margins and significance levels. On the external test set, sensitivities were similarly compared. dLI-RADS was non-inferior to LI-RADS for lesion-level accuracy in the internal evaluation set, achieving 80% accuracy compared with 74% for LI-RADS (p = 0.04)...

infographic.key_insight: For liver lesions ≤40 mm, dLI-RADS achieved 80% internal lesion-level accuracy versus 74% for LI-RADS, meeting the study’s non-inferiority criterion (p = 0.04).
infographic.clinical_relevance: Interpretable AI could support more consistent assessment of small liver lesions on multiphase CT for early hepatocellular carcinoma detection.
method: Analyzes manually segmented liver lesions on multiphase CT.
Combines neural network predictions with quantitative measurements reflecting LI-RADS major imaging features.
Uses logistic regression to estimate hepatocellular carcinoma probability.
infographic.evidence_signal: This multicenter retrospective study used histology for hepatocellular carcinoma and a composite reference for other lesions, with internal accuracy assessed using 10,000-repetition bootstrap non-inferiority tests.
infographic.watch_item: Manual segmentation may limit workflow scalability, and the supplied abstract does not report external-test performance results.
infographic.paper_title: An interpretable deep learning method for early hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis on multiphase CT

title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
authors: Andrew Zhang, Trinh T. L. Vuong, Sophia J. Wagner, Dongmin Bang, Tong Ding, Yuchang Su
abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.

infographic.key_insight: Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter model, makes fast, typed judgments from patient records while generalist language models formulate questions and synthesize evidence.
infographic.clinical_relevance: CS1 could support population-scale record review and clinical-trial screening, with answer probabilities helping route uncertain cases to human review.
method: Trained on 12.4 million question–answer pairs from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system.
Answers multiple typed questions in one forward pass without task-specific retraining.
Pairs with language-model agents for cited longitudinal-record answers and trial-eligibility screening.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1 outperformed open decision models up to 27B parameters on 13 of 14 independently scored tasks; across 21 external datasets, it approached the strongest tested 27B model’s aggregate performance with 6.4× faster inference in a matched workload.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective validation and local probability calibration remain important before deployment; the abstract does not establish improved patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
